misreading.wrong: God saves each soul directly and immediately; the individual alone is real, so Church, sacrament, and history are dispensable intermediaries.
misreading.right: There is no mere individual: man is himself only within the whole—mankind, history, cosmos—so Christianity serves all, and therefore stakes everything on Jesus.
misreading.quote: The individual is the salvation of the whole, and the whole receives its salvation only from the individual

argument.tension: God can save the mere individual directly; yet Christianity exists for history, community—the whole—and needs intermediaries.
argument.move: He denies the premise: no mere individual exists; since man lives within the whole, the whole's salvation must come through one individual.
argument.payoff: The scandal of Jesus as the world's savior becomes love's intrinsic logic, and the six structures of Christianity coalesce in love.

rubric: No mere individual exists; humans are inherently communal
Christianity serves all of history, not isolated souls
Therefore everything hangs on the one individual, Jesus

misreading.wrong: The Virgin Birth grounds Christ's divinity: God is literally his father, making Jesus a half-divine being like pagan savior-children.
misreading.right: Divine Sonship is ontological, in God's eternity—not biological; the virginal conception is the sign of salvation as God's new creation, sheer gift.
misreading.quote: the Divine Sonship of which faith speaks is not a biological but an ontological fact

argument.tension: The birth narrative appears to ground Christ's divinity; yet the Church says his Sonship does not rest on it at all.
argument.move: He separates them: Sonship rests on the Abba-Son dialogue—ontological in God's eternity; the birth narrative is Israel's barren-mother theology of grace.
argument.payoff: The Virgin Birth becomes a sign that salvation is pure gift—new creation, not divine biology—and Mary fulfills Israel's hope of grace.

rubric: Sonship is ontological, not biological
Virginal conception signifies salvation as sheer gift
New creation: God's Word amid barren humanity

misreading.wrong: The Cross appeases an angry God whose justice demands an infinite sacrifice: the Son's death pays the debt sinners owe.
misreading.right: The Cross is movement from above: God reconciles the world to himself, giving himself—love's self-offering, not a price paid to appease wrath.
misreading.quote: God does not wait until the guilty come to be reconciled; he goes to meet them and reconciles them.

argument.tension: Scripture holds both God's descent to reconcile and Christ's offering to the Father; the payment picture distorts both directions.
argument.move: He reads Hebrews: Christ's profane execution was the world's one cosmic liturgy, replacing all sacrificial offerings with the self-gift of love.
argument.payoff: Worship becomes thanksgiving and receptivity; the Cross reveals who God is—self-giving love—and who man is—needing grace.

rubric: Cross descends: God reconciles sinners first
Sacrifice is self-giving love, not destruction
Worship is Eucharist: receiving, not compensating God

misreading.wrong: The article describes a mythological underworld beneath the earth where souls are tortured—the hell of popular imagination, now obsolete.
misreading.right: 'Hell' translates sheol, the state of the dead: Christ entered death's final loneliness, so now love dwells in death; only self-enclosure is hell.
misreading.quote: Death is absolute loneliness. But the loneliness into which love can no longer advance is—hell.

argument.tension: Death is the silent void where no voice reaches—God seems absent; the article looks like discardable cosmological myth.
argument.move: Reading it through Holy Saturday and Christ's death cry, he finds God present in God-forsakenness: solidarity with the dead at the bottom.
argument.payoff: Death is hell no longer—love dwells in it; only deliberate self-enclosure remains hell, the 'second death'.

rubric: Hell means final loneliness, not torture
Christ descends into death's abandonment with us
Only self-imposed enclosure remains hell

misreading.wrong: The resurrection means Jesus' corpse was revived and returned to ordinary earthly life—a biological miracle that simply reverses death's process.
misreading.right: He rose to definitive life—zoe beyond bios—a new mode of being, recognized only in appearances: the crucified one, touched yet untouchable.
misreading.quote: it is zoe, new, different, definitive life; life that has stepped beyond the mortal realm of bios and history

argument.tension: Love demands indestructibility yet cannot grant it within mortal bios; the appearances describe one both recognized and unrecognizable.
argument.move: He reads the narratives' dialectic—touching and not touching, same yet transformed—as the very form of life beyond biological laws.
argument.payoff: Resurrection is love proven stronger than death; since his love embraces all, his rising is the ground of our immortality.

rubric: Risen life is zoe, a new mode
Not resuscitation: no return to bios
His love for all grounds our rising

misreading.wrong: The Ascension means Jesus flew up into the sky and left the world—a three-story cosmos with 'up' as a real direction.
misreading.right: Ascension is Christ's being with God; heaven is the contact of man with God—so in him God has time and is near to all.
misreading.quote: Heaven is to be defined as the contact of the being “man” with the being “God”

argument.tension: Modern physics cancels 'above' and 'below', making ascent mythical; yet prayer needs a God who is present and responsive in time.
argument.move: He recasts ascent as the upper dimension of human existence—contact with God—so eternity is contemporary with every present.
argument.payoff: In Jesus, God has time for the world; he is the throne of grace one may approach at any time.

rubric: Heaven is God-human contact, not location
Being with God makes Christ universally near
The Ascension grounds the possibility of prayer

misreading.wrong: Final judgment is the opposite of love: a terrifying reckoning that cancels grace, reducing Christianity to fear and moral bookkeeping.
misreading.right: Judgment preserves justice as love's excess—and the judge is our brother Jesus, so over judgment glows the dawn of hope.
misreading.quote: True love is excess of justice, excess that goes farther than justice, but never destruction of justice

argument.tension: Grace promises pure gift; judgment demands account of works—the two cannot be dissolved into each other without loss.
argument.move: He holds them in paradox: freedom means responsibility before someone—and that someone is the crucified brother who has suffered.
argument.payoff: Judgment keeps life serious and preserves justice; because Jesus is judge, the article tinges judgment with hope, not terror.

rubric: Freedom grounds responsibility; judgment protects it
Love exceeds justice but never destroys it
Our judge is the brother Jesus—hope

misreading.wrong: The Creed is a list of timeless truths about Christ—propositions to affirm—rather than the narration and interpretation of events.
misreading.right: The articles narrate and interpret one event—God's path with us; faith hangs on the happening, and without the event the words are empty.
misreading.quote: They are the interpretation of an event; if this event is removed, they become empty talk

argument.tension: Abstract doctrines look more modern than a story of descent, death, and glory; yet disembodied faith loses contact with reality.
argument.move: He shows the sequence—conception, Cross, descent, rising, glory, return—spans the total range of existence: divinity descending, humanity taken into God.
argument.payoff: History becomes revelation's medium; each article is one stage of God's single self-giving movement of love.

rubric: Each article interprets a real event
The sequence traces one movement of love
Faith confesses happenings, not abstractions

misreading.wrong: The Creed's last articles—Church, communion, forgiveness, resurrection—are four separate beliefs loosely appended after the story of Christ.
misreading.right: All are developments of one profession, 'I believe in Holy Spirit': God's saving power at work in history through baptism, Eucharist, transformation.
misreading.quote: nothing more than developments of its basic profession, “I believe in Holy Spirit.”

argument.tension: The Spirit article seems third-Person doctrine; the following articles seem practical add-ons—as if belief and practice pulled apart.
argument.move: He recovers the Greek text's salvation-historical sense: the Spirit is God's gift to history, and each later article concretizes his working.
argument.payoff: Salvation history and the Trinity interlock again: the Church appears sacramentally, as the Spirit's activity—baptism, Eucharist, final transformation.

rubric: Last articles develop one belief: the Spirit
The Spirit is God's power in history
Each names his working: sacraments, transformation

misreading.wrong: The Church is the community of the perfect; her holiness rests on members' virtue, and her scandals disprove her claim to it.
misreading.right: Holiness is God's sanctifying power at work despite sinners—grace's paradoxical shape; 'catholic' means visibly one around one Word and one bread.
misreading.quote: that power of sanctification which God exerts in her in spite of human sinfulness

argument.tension: The Creed calls the Church holy and one; history shows failure and division—the formula seems to deny plain experience.
argument.move: He turns the objection: true holiness is union and redeeming love—God mixing with the dirt; holiness together with unholiness is grace's shape.
argument.payoff: The Church comforts rather than condemns—word heard, sacrament celebrated, forbearance shared—and catholicity demands visible oneness in a torn world.

rubric: Holiness is God's gift despite human sin
Catholicity: visible unity—one Word, one bread
True holiness unites and redeems, not separates

misreading.wrong: The immortal soul is what really survives; 'resurrection of the body' is a crude mythological add-on about physical corpses being reassembled.
misreading.right: Biblical resurrection affirms the whole embodied person—awakened by God's love, in fellowship—and matter's future: not Greek soul-survival, nor restored physical bodies.
misreading.quote: not by virtue of their own power, but because they are known and loved by God

argument.tension: Greek deathless-soul fits modern minds but abandons the body; literal resurrection of flesh offends modern physics—both answers look impossible.
argument.move: He removes the Greek-biblical overlay: Paul teaches resurrection of persons in transformed form—dialogic immortality, awakening by God's love.
argument.payoff: The whole person and matter have a future; fellowship persists, and 'soul' is re-grounded as being God's partner in dialogue.

rubric: Whole person rises, not separable soul
Awakening: held in being by God's love
Transformed person, not restored physical body

misreading.wrong: The Holy Spirit is a vague feeling of religious enthusiasm—a pious atmosphere—not a distinct divine power whose coming reshapes faith and Church.
misreading.right: The Spirit is the risen Christ's living presence—love stronger than death—who personalizes faith through forgiveness and gathers believers into one body.
misreading.quote: the Holy Spirit as the power through which the risen Lord remains present in the history of the world

argument.tension: Spirit-teaching drifts into vague edification; Church-teaching turns institutional—split apart, both lose their function in Christian consciousness.
argument.move: He holds them together: the Spirit is God's power in history; the Church is his sacramental activity—forgiveness creating communion.
argument.payoff: Faith becomes personal and ecclesial at once: one bread, one body; the Spirit is love that overleaps death, transforming world to resurrection.

rubric: The Spirit is Christ's living presence in history
He personalizes: forgiveness creates communion
Spirit and Church inseparable—word and sacrament

misreading.wrong: Faith is a blind leap into the irrational—believing what contradicts reason, a private feeling set against knowledge and evidence.
misreading.right: Faith is stand-understand: entrusting myself to the ground I did not make—the logos, truth itself—where believing, trusting, and loving become one.
misreading.quote: its central formula is not “I believe in something”, but “I believe in you.”

argument.tension: Practical knowledge makes and proves; meaning cannot be made or proven—yet man cannot live without meaning.
argument.move: He distinguishes planes: belief stands on received ground; understanding grows only from belief—so faith fulfills reason instead of canceling it.
argument.payoff: The Creed's 'I believe' and 'Amen' converge in 'I believe in you'—the discovery of God in the face of Jesus.

rubric: Faith stands on ground not self-made
Believing, trusting, loving fuse in a You
Faith enables understanding; not irrational escape
